about: Synthetic, built to keep the sentence structures of the owner's real agency letter of 2026-09-28 with none of its names or numbers and in other words: a follow-up to a phone call, a limits sentence citing an asterisked section of the agreement with a conditional 'requires', a capitalised NOT, 'Even though you are NOT privileged ...', 'This means that if you are required to provide urgent surgical care (an em-dash aside) ..., that care is treated as ...', a closing that the sender is taking it up with the hospital, and a signature with a degree, a title and phone numbers in Gmail's link form. Hard-wrapped as mail is. On the rules before 2026-09-29 it failed as the real letter did: read as asking (mixed here, for its attachment), with one invented ask of kind unknown quoting the conditional clause. It asks for nothing. Target: one insurance record, the start taken from the attached agreement's 'effective as of' date.
subject: Liability coverage question
body:
Dr. Testa,

Following up on our call this afternoon about your liability coverage.
Under your Locum Services Agreement, the professional liability policy follows the work you do
within the bounds of your assignment and the privileges the hospital granted you. Your agreement does NOT
carve out obstetric emergencies or limit which patients you may treat in one. In *Section 4.1
(Professional Liability Coverage)* of your agreement, Brightwater Locum Partners provides professional
liability insurance for work on each Assignment at $2,000,000 per claim and a $4,000,000 annual
aggregate, or more if a state statute requires it.



Nothing in the agreement puts *a limit on emergency care* that sits inside your clinical
privileges. As an *independent contractor using your own clinical judgment (Section 3.2),* your cover
reaches work within your training (here, General Surgery), your licensure, and emergencies. Even though
you are NOT privileged by the hospital to perform cesarean deliveries, an urgent situation there
still counts as insured work. This means that if you are required to provide urgent surgical care—an
operation you would not normally do there—while working inside your licence, that care is treated as
*insured clinical work*, on the usual terms of the policy.


Riley and I are taking this up with the hospital's medical staff office, and it should not come up
again.

Devon Marsh, MHA

Senior Recruiter, General Surgery and Trauma Team



*Brightwater Locum Partners*

Non-clinical administrative work sits outside that insurance.
